parties:
Rupali Bank Limited Dhaka ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Artha Rin Adalat Dhaka and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Nozrul Islam Chowdhury J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to "why the impugned order No. 10 dated 5-10-2005 passed by the respondent No. 1 (Annexure-A) shall not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why respondent No. 1 shall not be directed to restore the execution case No. 423 of 2005 to its original file and number for proceeding with the same in accordance with law. 

2. Facts in a nutshell, out of which this Rule arises, are that Title Suit No. 90 of 1992 brought by the petitioner Rupali Bank Ltd as plaintiff impleading W Rahman Jute Mills Ltd and seven of its Directors as defendants for recovery of loan by sale, of the mortgaged property, amounting to Taka 22,15,91,799.61. The said suit eventually ended with a compromise petition filed jointly by both the parties as such a compromise decree was passed in the said suit on January 26, 1995. The aforesaid decree was passed with the direction as under:— 

Balance amount of Taka 14,93,72,630 (Taka fourteen crores ninety three lacs seventy two thousand six hundred thirty only) shall constitute as principal amount to be paid by the defendant in 15 (fifteen) years beginning from 1st July 1993 but repayment shall commence from 1st January 1996 including interest at the rate of 3% per annum on the outstanding dues also from 1st July 1996 to be calculated quarterly and in default to pay any installment by the defendants all the benefits given above shall be treated as cancelled and the defendants shall be liable to pay the entire dues including interest at bank's usual rate till realization." 

3. With the direction as above, 15 years installments were granted by the compromise decree allowing payment of installments. 

4. The defendant respondents of that suit paid upto its 8th installments, thereafter, stopped payment consequently, compromise decree as aforesaid ceased to exist, therefore, the Rupali Bank as decree holder of that suit brought Execution Case No. 423 of 2005 on 8-6-2005 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka i.e. respondent No. 1 of this writ petition. 

5. During pendency of the aforesaid execution case the defendant judgment-debtor filed an application under section 28 of the Artha Rin Adalat AM, 2003 with a prayer for dismissal of the execution case on the ground of limitation. The said application was resisted by the petitioner decree holder but after hearing both sides the learned Joint District Judge as executing court passed the impugned order dated 5-10-2005 holding that the execution application i.e. Artha Jari Case No. 423 of 2005 be dismissed as it is barred by limitation under section 28 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003. 

6. The said order dated 5-10-2005 passed by the respondent No. 1 is in challenge in this rule. 

7. Mr Sk Md Morshed, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Imam Hasan and Mr Niaz Morshed having taken us through the entire writ petition including the papers annexed therewith submits that the respondent No. 1 while passing the impugned order misconstrued the relevant provision of law applicable in the instant case thereby misdirected itself in passing the impugned order which tantamount to an order without lawful authority which is of no legal effect. 

8. Elaborating his submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that as per the direction of the trial court in the compromise decree the judgment-debtor respondent having failed to pay the requisite installments as per stipulation of the trial court, rendered the solenama decree nugatory, in other words, the solenama decree ceased to exist on and from 30-6-2002 for non-payment of stipulated installments by the judgment-debtor and the execution case was filed on 8-6-2005 well within 3(three) years from the date of accrual of the cause of action on 30-6-2002 as per Article 182 of the Limitation Act which provides a period of 3(three) years for the purpose of execution of a decree. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits further that since cause of action arose prior to coming into force of Artha Rin AIN, 2003 therefore, the decree holder is at liberty to go for execution of the decree under the repealed law which provides applicability of both Civil Procedure Code and the Limitation Act, therefore, in the instant execution case Article 182 is applicable and not section 28 of Artha Rin Adalat AIN, 2003. And by an application of the same provision of law in the instant case the respondent No.1 acted without lawful authority in having passed the impugned order upon such erroneous application of law rather the same is without lawful authority which has no legal effect. 

9. It is also submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that in the event of bringing the execution case prior to commencement of Artha Rin Adalat AIN, 2003 in that case too sub-section(3) of section 60 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain could not be applied, bringing the same within the purview of the new enactment. Therefore, the execution case has been brought as per repealed law of the land for the purpose where application of the new law is not permissible. 

10. Mr Sk Morshed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits further that section 6 (clause C and E) of the General Clauses Act protect the instant Execution Case No. 423 of 2005 and the dismissal thereof on the point of limitation as per the impugned order is of no legal effect. 

11. The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly submits that section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain provides 90 days for an appeal against the judgment and decree only but not against any interlocutory order, therefore, the petitioner rightly invoked the writ jurisdiction of this court and obtained the present rule which is very much maintainable under the facts and circumstances of this case. 

12. On the other hand, Mr Fida M Kamal the learned advocate appearing with Mr Sajed Ahmed Sami submits that in view of section 41 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 appeal lies against the order but no writ petition is maintainable against the same and in view of the fact that the execution case in which the impugned order was passed, was brought after the commencement of Artha Rin Adalat AIN, 2002, the provision of section 41 of the Artha Rin Ain, 2003 is very much applicable therefore the learned Advocate submits that the rule is liable to be discharged on the ground of maintainability. 

13. It is also submitted by the learned Advocate for the respondent that section 28 provides a period of one year from the date of passing of the decree or order subject to the provision of section 29 of the said Act and the instant execution case has been brought long after the period prescribed by section 28 read with section 29 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, the executing court has rightly dismissed the case on the ground of limitation by the impugned order which do not call for any interference by this court in exercise of its writ jurisdiction therefore, the rule is liable to be discharged. 

14. It is also submitted by the learned Advocate for the respondents that the period of limitation is ordinarily a matter of procedural law, and when a question of limitation is raised it ought to be decided in accordance with law in force at the time of institution of the suit and not that in force at the time of accrual of cause of action unless there is any express provision to the contrary in the law itself. Therefore, section 6 of the General Clauses Act would not apply and the period of limitation prescribed by an act would govern the case. 

15. Substantiating his submission the learned Advocate for the respondents placed reliance in the case of Bank of India vs Md Muhammad Ashraf reported in PLD 1965 (WP) Karachi 69. 

16. It is also submitted by the learned Advocate for the respondents that where a statute is repealed and a new statute takes place for the same purpose, the action under the repealed statutes continues but that does not mean that the procedure under the repealed enactment must be followed. The statute dealing with matters of procedure may properly have retrospective effect unless that construction be textually inadmissible. Substantiating his submission the learned Advocate for the respondents placed reliance in the case of Angles Corporation (Pvt) Ltd vs Bangladesh reported in 59 DLR 601. 

17. We have heard the learned Advocates from both sides, perused the petition and the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondents including the materials annexed therewith. We have also gone through the two decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the respondents wherefrom it is apparent that the substantial question has been raised in this writ petition as to whether Artha Rin Execution Case No. 423 of 2005 filed before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka should be governed by the law namely, Artha Rin Adalat Ain,1990 or the amended Act thereto by Artha Rin Ain, 2003 and in answering the question we may refer to the background of this writ petition which arose out of an execution case of Artha Rin Adalat and the execution case was brought on the basis of solenama decree in Title Suit No. 90 of 1992 and in the said execution case there was a direction upon the judgment-debtor to pay the installments as per direction of the court with stipulation that in the event of failure on the part of the judgment-debtor to pay the installment in that event the facilities granted under the solenama decree or for that matter the very fact of the said solenama decree ceases to exist and the decree holder shall be at liberty to proceed with the execution case for realization of the entire amount claimed in the suit and on perusal of the materials on record we find that on and from 30-6-2002 solenama decree has been rendered nugatory, therefore, cause of action to go for execution of the decree arose on that particular date namely 30-6-2002 while the execution case No. 423 of 2005 was instituted on 8-6-2005. Therefore, Article 182 of the Limitation Act shall apply in the instant case which provides limitation for 3(three) years although as a matter of fact Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 came into operation on and from 1-5-2003. It is not the case that the execution case was initiated prior to the new enactment rather it is the case that the execution was brought into being about 2 years after the new enactment. Petitioners, in the writ petition further urge that since cause of action in the execution case arose prior to the new enactment of Artha Rin Ain, 2003 the execution case shall be governed by the repealed law i.e. Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. In this connection we feel it proper to go through the case relied upon by the respondents namely Bank of India vs Muhammad Ashraf reported in PLD 1965 (WP) Karachi 69 wherefrom it appears, upon consideration of the main decision of Indian jurisdiction as well as of Pakistan including those of Privy Council, it has been held that the most important principle is that period of limitation is ordinarily a matter of procedure only, and that when a question of limitation is raised it ought to be decided in accordance with the law of limitation in force at the time of the institution of the suit and not that in force at the time of the cause of action unless there be any express provision to the contrary in the Act itself. The other decision referred by the learned Advocate for the respondent is the case of Angles Corporation (Pot) Ltd. vs Bangladesh reported in 59 DLR 601. Upon a consideration of the decision referred to above, and upon close scrutiny of the materials available in this writ petition we are in respectful agreement with the view taken in that particular case to the effect that the period of limitation is ordinarily a matter of procedure only, and that a question of limitation if raised it ought to be decided in accordance with the law of limitation in force at the time of institution of the suit or proceeding and not that in force at the time of cause of action arose and there being no express provision to the contrary is available in the repealed Act namely Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003. We are of the considered opinion that the question of limitation would be decided as per the law in force, available at the institution of the proceeding and not from the cause of action. Therefore, we find no substance in this rule accordingly. Therefore, we find that the question of limitation as has been decided by the executing court calls for no interference by this court. 

18. Turning to the question of maintainability of the writ petition as has been raised by the learned Advocate for the respondent we may safely refer to the provision of section 41 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 which provides, an appeal shall lie both against the decree or order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in a proceeding and the impugned order has been passed in execution proceeding by the Artha Rin Adalat, appeal could have been brought by the aggrieved party and there is no scope for challenging the same invoking the writ jurisdiction of this court. 

19. In this connection we may take recourse to the principal of law enunciated in the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) vs Artha Rin Adalat reported in 59 DLR (AD) 6 wherefrom it appears that their lordships while disposing of a question of similar nature (of course under the repealed law) decided in the language as under :-

"In view of the decisions quoted above we are led to irresistible conclusion that there being specific remedy in the statute for filing appeal against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat in the present case the defendant not availing of the aforesaid remedy cannot maintain the writ petitions." 

20. In view of the position as above, we are also of the opinion that the rule is liable to be discharged on the ground of maintainability as well. 

In view of what has been stated above, we find no substance in this rule. Hence, it is discharged without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
The was Rule issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2008 and 31-8-2008 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 disallowing the appeal affirming those dated 20-11-2006 and 27-11-2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the original suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession being Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 in the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Patuakhali, contending inter alia that the suit property appertaining to Mouza Kudbar Char under Mirjaganj police station corresponding to CS Khatian No. 145 measuring an area of 4.12 acres of land originally belonged to one Kasem Ali Kha and Kazem Ali Kha. The CS record was correctly prepared in their names. The original owners died issueless and the property devolved upon their cousin Arman Kha. In the CS Khatian No. 142 the land measuring 8.25 acres have been recorded in the name of Arman Kha. At the demise of Arman Kha his three sons namely Ismail Kha, Asmat Kha and Jonab. Ali Kha inherited the property. In the petty settlement Khatian Nos. 108, 140/2 measuring 3.29 acres of land was recorded in the names of three brothers. Ismail Kha died leaving two daughters Jarina and Urful Nessa and two full brothers Asmat and Jonab All Kha. Urful died leaving behind one son, two daughters who are the plaintiff Nos. 41, 42 and 43. The plaintiffs who are 44 in numbers are the heirs and successive heirs of the recorded owners who possess the suit land for more than 12 years without any break. During settlement operation 2.25 acres of land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and the rest has been recorded in the names of the defendants. The plaintiffs have got their paternal homestead in the suit property. The defendants have no manner of title, interest and possession over the suit land but on the basis of wrong SA record they denied the title of the plaintiffs which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit.

3. The contrary case of the defendant in short is thus that the superior landlord of the plaintiffs' predecessors was MT Brown Estate under Court of Wards and the land of CS Khatian No. 145 was auction purchased by the superior landlord. Beside this the land of CS Khatian No. 142 was also sold in a certificate case and was purchased by the superior landlord. The Court of Wards took possession of the land through court against which the predecessor of the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 139 of 1945 challenging the auction sale which was dismissed for default. Subsequently, the Court of Wards granted settlement in favour of one Jonab Ali by granting 'dakhilas' and those properties have been recorded in the name of the defendants during Revisional Settlement and State Acquisition operation. The land of Petty Settlement Khatian No. 108 was purchased by the government and the government resettled the same in part to the defendants and in part to the plaintiffs. Apart from this, the land of PS Khatian No. 140/2 was auction purchased by government for arrear of rent and the government leased out the same to the predecessor of the defendant Jonab Ali and one Nawab Ali Mia. The further case of the defendants is such that the SA Khatian has been correctly prepared in their names and they had been owning and possessing the suit land after construction of homestead and they have donated 0.30 acres of land in favour of the government for establishment of a 'Hat'.

4. The learned trial court after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the suit on contest on 20-11-2006. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 in the Court of learned District Judge, Patuakhali which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali and the learned lower appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners has preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of status quo.

6. Mr Abdul Quayum with Mr Abdul Matin Khasru, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr AJ Mohammad Ali with Mr JN Deb the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite-parties.

7. The learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that both the courts below in passing the judgment and dismissal decree and in disallowing the appeal committed illegality and irregularity resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocates further submits that none of the courts considered the facts of the case as to the effect that no paper has been filed to substantiate the delivery of possession pursuant to alleged settlement in favour of defendant-opposite parties. There has been total non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning miscarriage of justice. There is no paper from the side of the defendants that MT Brown Estate ever managed the property under the management of court of Wards and there is no evidence to show that the alleged settlement was granted in favour of the defendant by the Court of Wards. Both the Courts below on surmise and conjecture holding the correctness of the alleged settlement and auction purchase committed error of law. Neither the trial court nor the appellate court considered that there is no evidence of annulment and taking possession of the land by the government. Petty Settlement Khatian marked Exhibits-'Ka-3' and 'Ka-4' shows that the government was not the land-lord which is also not considered by the courts below. It was the case of the plaintiffs that Jonab Ali the predecessor of the defendants created the papers of auction and settlement by the act of fraud and forgery which has vitiated the alleged auction and settlement. The learned Advocates also submit that the courts below misdirected themselves on the question of payment of rent which is on the basis of wrong SA Khatian which has no presumptive value of correctness. The courts below also not considered the evidence of the defendant's witness No.6 who has admitted the possession of the plaintiff-petitioners and their homestead. The learned Advocates lastly submit that it is the case of the defendants that they took pattan from the landlord through 'amaldari dakhila' not by kabuliat. The CS khatian is a title document which proves the bona fide of the plain-tiffs and the evidence adduced from the side of the parties not properly assessed by the learned lower appellate court in its true perspective and there is non-reading and misreading of evidence and non-consideration to material facts in disposing the appeal which is violative to the provisions laid down under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable.

8. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsels of the petitioners the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule submits that the defendants admit the CS Khatian in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor-in-interest They also admit the title of Arman Kha. But the fact remains that MT Brown Estate the superior landlord for arrear of rent auction purchased the suit land. Subsequently, the defendants were granted settlement. The learned Advocates further submits that both the courts below concurrently held that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for since they have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property. The learned Advocates also submit that the plaintiffs to the suit by subsequent amendment of their plaint challenged the settlement and auction purchase of the defendants in their pleadings. Therefore, the onus of proof totally lies upon the plaintiffs to disprove the auction purchase and settlement of the defendants. The plaintiffs during trial of the original suit failed to discharge their onus in proving their pleading. The learned Advocates lastly submits that the plaintiffs have admitted after amending their original plaint that the recent khatians i.e. record of rights has not been prepared in their names but has been prepared in the names of the defendants. Those khatians have been wrongly prepared, which is the case of the plaintiffs and as a result of that the onus of proof is on the plaintiffs to prove that the SA khatian is wrongly prepared in the names of the defendants. The plaintiffs to the suit also alleged that the certificate sale, auction purchase and subsequent settlement taken by the defendants from the auction purchasers are fraudulent, collusive and not acted upon. Therefore, obviously under sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act the onus of proof is on the plaintiffs to prove their respective plea i.e. their case which does not lie on the defendants. Even then, the defendants under the provisions of Evidence Act after calling the volume book and necessary papers showing the certificate sale and auction purchase proved their case and after adducing evidence to that effect have proved that the tenancy of the original owners have been extinguished by virtue of auction sale as cited from the side of the defendants. All the documentary evidence has been properly evaluated by both the courts below and all the evidence on records has been properly assessed in its true perspective before arrival at a decision as to the merit of the suit and its subsequent appeal. There is no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with.

9. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case record exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses and all other connected papers.

10. On perusal of the case record it transpires that during trial of the original suit both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective pleadings. It is an admitted position that the CS khatian Nos. 142 and 45 corresponding to RS khatian Nos. 108 and 140/2 marked Exhibits-1, 1(Ka), 1(Kha) and l(Ga) stands recorded in the names of Kazem Ali Kha. It is also admitted from the sides of the respective parties that the plaintiffs are the heirs and successive heirs of the CS and PS recorded tenants. It is the specific contention of the contesting defendants that the land of CS khatian Nos. 142 and 145 was put into certificate proceedings being Nos. 149 and 150 of 1933-34 and in that certificate cases the property was put to an auction. The superior landlord MT Brown Estate auction purchased the same which was duly affected on 20-6-1934 AD. In support of this the defendant-opposite parties produced the bainanama of the certificate proceeding marked Exhibit-'Ga' and 'Gha'. Besides this, it is apparent from the face of the records that during pendency of the original suit under the purview of Evidence Act to prove the certified copy of the bainanama the defendants called for the volume books from Patuakhali Sub-registry office. The concerned record-keeper after bringing the volume books proved the same which go on to show that one Poresh Nath Sen, Manager, Court of Wards on behalf of MT Brown Estate auction purchased the land in dispute. It is also evident from the documents on record that the predecessor of the plaintiffs for cancellation of the auction sale instituted a Title Suit being No. 129 of 1945 in the 3rd Court of the then Munsif, Patuakhali. That suit was dismissed for default. For restoration of the suit the plaintiffs to that suit preferred a Miscellaneous Case being No. 264 of 1946 which was also dismissed on 25-7-1946. To substantiate the aforesaid facts the certified copy of the Suit Register was produced which are Exhibit-'Uma' and 'Cha' respectively. It is the concurrent findings and decision of the courts below that the title of the plaintiffs predecessors has been extinguished by virtue of certificate proceeding and auction sale and in this way the plaintiffs having no manner of right, title and interest in the disputed property are not in a position to get the relief sought for.

11. It is a fact that the SA record of rights has got no presumptive value of correctness but it would prevail until and unless it is rebutted. While both the parties adduced evidence in support of their pleadings the onus of proof under the ambit of Evidence Act lies on the parties to prove their respective cases as stated in their pleadings. Consulting the case records it is obvious, to note that the primary onus of proof which was upon the defendants was discharged in proving their bonafide but vis-a-vis despite the pleadings of the defendants have been specifically challenged and denied by the plaintiffs by subsequent amendment of their plaint but that onus of proof was not discharged by producing cogent, tangible evidence from the plaintiff's side. Having gone through the records I find that the witnesses produced from the sides of the parties have been properly assessed by the Courts below. The trial court in his observation and findings discussed the testimony of the witnesses and scrutinizing the evidence on records it is noticed that the plaintiff No.  26 Abdul Latif Khan as witness No. 1 tried to establish their case who deposed on behalf of all the plaintiffs. This witness admits in his deposition that the RS and SA khatians stands recorded in the name of the defendants and prior to this despite he denied that their predecessor-in-interest for setting aside the certificate cases instituted a Title Suit being No. 139 of 1944 which was dismissed on 20-6-1946 and against that the Miscellaneous Case No. 246 of 2006 was also dismissed but the fact remains that the documentary evidence which are produced makes it clear that the predecessor of the plaintiffs actually for cancellation of the certificate proceeding instituted the suit but failed. To substantiate the position of the plaintiffs they have adduced two witnesses and consulting their testimony it can be easily held that they have hopelessly failed to prove the plaintiffs title and possession as alleged over the disputed property. They even do not know the disputed property practically. On the contrary, the defendants in support of their case examined 5(five) witnesses. All the witnesses have been thoroughly discussed by the trial court in his observation and findings and I find nothing non-consideration, misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-appreciation of the actual position of law. It is the established principle of Civil Law that the plaintiffs shall have to stand on their own legs and they cannot bank upon their adversary. In the instant suit after consulting evidence I have the reason to incline such a view that the plaintiffs' to the suit have failed to discharge their onus in proving their respective pleadings.

<u>12. Consulting the case records it appears that no such material contradiction, omission or perverse findings is noticed by dint of which it can be held that there has been any sort of illegality in deciding the fate of the suit and its subsequent appeal. In our revisional jurisdiction, scope of interference under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is very limited. Only where it is noticed that there has been misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts or the observation and findings is based upon gross misconception of law or otherwise perverse which is contrary to law, evidence and records; only in that case the judgment and decree of the appellate court can be interfered with. In the instant case as I have already discussed earlier, no such material is transpired by which I can draw such interference that the impugned judgment and decree deserve my interference.</u>

13. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs, the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2008 and 31-8-2008 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali, in Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 disallowing the appeal affirming those dated 20-11-2006 and 27-11-2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 is hereby affirmed.

14. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment and order at once and send down the lower Court's records immediately.

End.

Vs.
Din Mohammad & ors
full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J: This revisional application is against the order dated 16.4.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1982 restoring the same to its file and number vacating the order dated 5.12.83 dismissing the case for non-prosecution.

2. The aforesaid order was passed upon an application filed under Section 151 of the  Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that the Miscellaneous Case was dismissed on 5.12.83 for non-prosecution on the basis of an application filed by the lawyer of the opposite parties without having been authorised to file such application and the said order was obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court.

3. Syed Mahmud Hussain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the impugned order is illegal inasmuch as an application under section 151 of the Code was not maintainable and there was no finding of fraud.

<u>4. The said Miscellaneous Case was filled for restoration of Title Suit No. 58 of 1980 decreed ex-parte on 30.12.81. The remedy available under section 151 of the Code is, not, so circumscribed in the present case as contended by the learned Advocate. Power given under Section 151 of the Code is available to a Court and it can pass an order in exercise of its inherent power to revise its own order obtained by a party by practice of fraud upon it in order prevent abuse of the process of the Court. But it would be otherwise where it is a case of fraud between the parties and the aggrieved party has a remedy by a separate suit. In this case before me as the opposite parties want to say that the order of dismissal of the Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1982 was obtained by practice of fraud upon the Court, the court passing the said order was competent to rectify the wrong by invoking the inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Proceeding. This view of mine finds support from the decision in the case of Abdul Majid Kha-Vs-Mahmudabi reported in 1949 Nag. 366 wherein it has been held that:</u>

<u>"The inherent powers may be exercised in a case where the court has been misled by fraud practised upon it because in such a case the court would be under a duty to correct its own proceedings which, in the absence of any other provision, it would do by resort to inherent powers. But when it is a case of fraud between the parties and the aggrieved party has another remedy of a suit open to it, there should be no occasion for invoking inherent powers of the Court".</u>

<u>Moreover in this case, if the Miscellaneous Case for restoration of the suit decreed ex-parte is restored and heard the petitioners will not be prejudiced either.</u>

5. It also seems to me that the learned Subordinate Judge after perusing the application, hearing the parties and considering the case of the petitioners passed the impugned order. In this view of the matter, I am of the opinion that he was satisfied regarding fraud practised upon him and thus it cannot be said that he has not considered the question of fraud, although he has not come to the finding to the effect in express term. As the impugned order passed on consideration of facts and circumstances of the case and the petitioners will not be prejudiced if the Miscellaneous Case is heard I think that the order complained of has been passed in all fairness to prevent abuse of the process of the Court.

For the reasons stated above, I am not inclined to interfere with the impugned order. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

Kad Banu & Ors ....... Appellants
Vs.
Hajera Khatun & Ors .......... Respondents
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. This appeal by way of special leave arises out of judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 340 of 1981.

2. Briefly the back ground of the case is as follows: Plaintiff-respondents filed Other Class Suit No. 28 of 1962 for permanent injunction in the Court of Munsif, Kishoreganj. The suit was decreed. On appeal by the defendants the appellate Court below set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and allowed the appeal. While the trial Court found the plaintiffs' possession the appellant Court below found the defendants' possession. In Second Appeal the High Court Division reversed the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below and restored those of the trial Court and decreed the suit. Be it noted that there was no stay order issued by the High Court Division during the pendency of the Second Appeal. Thereafter the plaintiffs put the decree into execution being Execution Case No. 37 of 1979 and in that proceeding the plaintiffs filed the application under Order 21 Rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure for attachment of the properties of the defendant and for civil imprisonment on the ground, inter alia, that the defendant had violated the order of permanent injunction and entered into the suit land forcibly in the first week of April, 1978. This application was filed on 4-9-79 and thereafter on 29-11-79 the defendant-judgment-debtors was directed to appear on 12-4-80 and in the meantime their properties were attached. The District Judge in revision took the view that the petition under order 21 Rule 32 was not maintainable and in that view of the matter allowed the revisional application. The High Court Division was moved under section 115(3) of the Code and the learned Single Judge in Civil Revision No. 340 of 1981 made the rule absolute after setting aside the order of the District Judge and affirmed the order of the trial court. The learned Single Judge noticed that the petition under Order 21 Rule 32 was maintainable independently inasmuch as Rule 32(1) C.P.C. provides an independent remedy to the decree holder in case the judgment-debtor violated the order of prohibitory injunction given in a decree by a Court.

3. Leave was granted to consider the question whether a petition under Order 21 Rule 32 was maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the case and whether the impugned order could be sustained.

4. As has been noticed that the Other Class Suit No. 28 of 1962 was decreed on 22-11-63 and the trial court found the plaintiffs' possession. The appellant Court set aside the decree and dismissed the suit and found defendants' possession. The High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 268 of 1963 restored and allowed the appeal and a significant observation was made which is as under:

“In view of the conflicting findings with regard to possession by the Courts below. I have given my anxions considerations whether to send back the appeal on remand for re-hearing. It appears that the suit out of which the present appeal arises was instituted as far back as in 1962 and the first appeal was disposed of in 1965. It will entail a good deal of hardship on the parties if the appeal is sent back on remand to the lower appellate Court after a lapse of 13 years. I have therefore, gone through the records of the case myself. Having regard to the evidence, both oral and documentary on record, I am satisfied that the plaintiffs and not the defendants Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are in possession of the suit land and accordingly they are entitled to the relief, prayed for.

Judgment of the High Court Division was pronounced on 2-3-78. While admitting the appeal under Order 41 Rule 11 C.P.C. no prayer was made for staying of the operation of the order of the appellate Court below. The appellate court below found possession in favour of the defendants. In this setting of fact the plaintiffs put the decree into execution and in that proceeding they brought the allegation that defendants had violated the order of injunction.

Order 21 Rule 32 is in the following terms : "Decree for specific performance for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction-(1) Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been passed, has bad an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced (in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction) by his detention in the Civil prison, or by the attachment of his property or by both".

This rule has a little history. Originally in 1882 section 260 was the equivalent rule. By amendment Act 29 of 1923 the words and expression "in the case of decree for restitution of conjugal rights by attachment of his property or in the case of decree for the specific performance or for an injunction" was inserted. In Protap Chunder Doss V. Peary Chowdhurain, 8 Cal. 174 section 260 was considered. It was observed:

“The proper course to pursue was to serve a notice on the judgment-debtor, directing him to comply with the order contained in the decree within a time to be fixed by such notice; and that if he failed to comply with such order within the time so limited, the Court might then, at the instance of the decree-holder, make an order either for the judgment-debtor's imprisonment or for the attachment of his property, due regard being had to the provision of section 260 in the latter case.

5. Mr. T. H. Khan appearing for the judgment debtor contended that in this case no opportunity was given to the judgment debtor for obeying any order of the court. He argued vigorously that the judgment of the High Court Division in Second Appeal clearly shows that on point of possession there was 'conflicting' decision the trial court holding that the plaintiff was in possession while the appellate court below found possession in favour of the defendants and the learned Single Judge made up his mind that the plaintiff was in possession and accordingly allowed the appeal without noticing that there was no stay order as against the order of lower appellate Court below. Consequently it is argued that when the judgment in Second Appeal was given it could not be said emphatically that the defendant was not in possession and in such circumstances it was imperative for the trial court to give an opportunity for obeying the order of High Court Division inasmuch as the rule it self said whether the parties against whom a decree for injunction, has been passed "has bad an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey "the decree may be enforced by detention in the civil prison or by attachment of his property or by both. In the given case emboldened by the decision of the High Court Division the plaintiff brought promptly the proceeding against the defendants for violation of injunction order and filed a petition under Order 21 Rule 32. No opportunity was given to the defendants for obeying the decree which was not signed till then. Section 260 reads as follows:

“When the party against whom a decree for specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for the performance of or abstention from any other particular act. has been made, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree or injunction and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced by his imprisonment, or by the attachment of his property, or by both.

In the case of Kishore Bun Mohunt V. Prosonna Coomar 21 Cal 74 the Privy Council had the occasion of considering the section.

6. In that case decree was not complied with which was passed in 1881. Thereafter the decree-holder filed an application under section 260 C.P.C. The Munsif gave the judgment in 1888 ordering the decree to be executed and on appeal the District Judge directed that the decree to be executed in part only. Both parties appealed to the High Court and the High Court affirmed the order for executing the decree. Thereafter in 1888 the decree holder filed petition for execution of the decree stating in their petition "that they had served the appellant with notice, and had presented themselves at the temple at certain times specified in the notice, in order that they might be allowed the opportunity of performing a certain ceremony and receiving certain articles necessary for its performance, and so afford the appellant an opportunity of complying with the decree." The Privy Council took the view that whatever defect was there that had been remedied by giving notice to the judgment debtor for complying with the decree and that fact of giving notice had settled the issue that the proceeding under section 260 was maintainable.

7. In Durga Das Nanda V. Deoraj Agarwala. 10 C.W.N. 297 the question was whether the notice to judgment debtor is obligatory in such case. In that case it was found that the judgment debtor had ample opportunity of obeying the decree and obeyed it for about 15 years when he without warning proceeded to act in defiance of it. The Court considered the case of Protap Chandra Das V. Peary Choudhrain. 8 Calcutta 174 and opined that there was no hard and fast rule that notice should be given as a matter of course. It was observed "but this does not show that in every case in which a decree-holder asked for relief under section 260, he must serve a notice upon the judgment debtor calling upon him to obey the decree, no doubt, if he takes this precaution and the judgment debtor fails to obey the decree the case against the latter is completely proved, but it is quite possible for the decree-holder even without service of notice to show conclusively that the judgment debtor had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it."

8. In the given case before us as has been noticed that the appellate Court below found possession of the defendants though the High Court in hesitant manner found possession of the plaintiff and in this setting when there was no stay order against the decision of the appellate court below which found the defendants' possession could it be said that the defendant acted in defiance of the order of the High Court Division in violating the order of injunction which was vacated by the appellate Court below and granted by the High Court Division. The sequence of events are to be looked into. The appellate Court below reversed the trial court's decree on 15-5-65 and the High Court Division restored the trial court's judgment and order in Second Appeal No. 268 of 1966 on 2-3-78 and then within a month the plaintiff decree holder brought the allegation of violating the injunction in April, 1978 and that petition was marked as the petition under Order 21 Rule 32 on 4-9-79. This fact speaks volume to support the contention of Mr. T.H. Khan that the defendants had no opportunity of obeying the decree of the High Court Division. We are not impressed by the submission that the decree was not drawn up till then but certainly the contention of the defendants that he had not violated any injunction order passed by the High Court Division which restored the trial court's order after 13 years deserves consideration inasmuch as his possession was found by the appellate Court below and during these thirteen years there is no positive evidence that the defendants were not in possession.

9. Admittedly no oral evidence was taken in this proceeding under Order 21 Rule 32. The learned Single Judge also observed-

"From the order dated 7-4-80 passed by the learned Munsif it does not appear that any witness was examined. The learned Munsif however perused the certified copies of the judgments of various courts and heard both the sides, which appears from the order itself. In that view of the matter I do not think that he passed the order without any application of mind or without looking into the records of the case.

With respect, this is not the correct approach to be made in a case under Order 21 Rule 32. It was imperative to find that the defendant had willfully disobeyed the order of the Court. A person disobeys an injunction not only when he fails to perform an act which is directed to do but when he does an act which he is prohibited from doing. There is as much disobedience in one case and the other, but as has been noticed in the Second Appeal the High Court Division simply found the possession of the plaintiff without making any further consequent order to deliver possession on the defendant whose possession was found by the appellate court below though the same was reversed by the High Court Division. To haul up the defendant for disobedience of injunction something more was necessary namely, evidence that he had knowledge of the High Court's order and deliberately disobeyed such order of that he had been served with notice of such order of the High Court Division and he willfully disobeyed such order. Anything short of this may pave the way for the contention which is now being made by the judgment debtor.

<u>10. Applying the principles mentioned above we are of the opinion that this appeal should be allowed and an opportunity should be given to prove the contention of the respective parties namely that the defendant had willfully disobeyed the order of injunction and evidence may be adduced by the respective parties.</u>

<u>11. In the result the appeal is allowed and the case is sent back on remand to trial court for disposal in accordance with law. There will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.

Abu Ahmed Abdul Hafiz and others ------ Petitioner
Vs.
M.A. Hoque Shirajee ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J: The question raised in this appeal by special leave is whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted in accordance with law while summarily disposing of an application under section 115(3) of the Civil Procedure Code upon expart hearing giving all the relief prayed for in that application but without issuing any rule upon the opposite-parties and without giving them any opportunity to be heard in the matter.

2. Appellants-landlords filed Title Suit No. 148 of 1964 in the First Court of Munsif, Sylhet for ejectment of the respondent, a monthly tenant and also for recovery of arrears of rent. The suit was decreed on 6 May 1957 upon rejection of all the contentions raised by the defendant-respondent. The decree was challenged before the District Judge by an appeal, but the appeal was also dismissed. Thereafter a second appeal was preferred before the High Court but it was also dismissed. A Petition for special leave to appeal was then filed before the then Supreme Court of Pakistan but leave was refused and the petition was dismissed by an order dated 3 December 1969.

3. The appellants-decree-holders, in an attempt to put the decree into execution, filed Title Execution Case No. 42 of 1967, but the respondent filed an application for striking off the Execution case alleging that the decree had been already adjusted. On hearing the decree-holders, the court rejected the application for striking off the execution proceeding holding that there was no adjustment of the decree at all but the application was filed by misrepresentation of facts. Thereafter the respondent filed an independent suit, Title Suit No. 301 of 1968 in the 1st Court of Munsif, for a declaration that the decree for his ejectment passed in Title Suit No. 148 of 1964 was illegal, void and inoperative, and in that suit the plaintiff-judgment-debtor also prayed for stay of all further proceedings of the Execution Case till disposal of the suit. The trial court by an order dated 20 February 1982 rejected the application for stay of the execution proceeding whereupon a revisional application was filed before the District Judge. The learned Additional District Judge who heard the matter, rejected the application refusing stay of the execution proceeding. Thereafter a second revisional application was filed before the High Court Division and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, without issuing any rule and without hearing these appellants passed the impugned order dated 30 March 1982 staying the Execution Case No. 42 of 1967 till disposal of the suit.

<u>4. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Advocate for the appellants has seriously assailed the impugned order of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division contenting that it is unwarranted by law and fact and that it is unjust and improper causing grave injustice to the appellants who have been deprived of the fruits of their decree without being given any opportunity to be heard in the matter. As has been stated above, the decree for ejectment as well as for realisation of a huge arrear of rent on the ground of default in the payment of rent, passed by the trial court on 6 May 1967, was challenged by the respondent at all stages and forums without any success and the decree was maintained as one having been passed in accordance with law. Thereafter, when the decree was sought to be executed an attempt was made by the respondent-tenant to get the execution proceeding struck off by deliberate misrepresentation that the decree had been otherwise adjusted, and when that attempt failed, the respondent filed the independent suit for a declaration that the decree for ejectment was void and illegal. The respondent may proceed with his suits, if so advised, but there is no reason whatsoever why the execution of the decree which was obtained in 1967 in a different suit should be stayed when the said decree was maintained all through. Mere filing of a suit, particularly in the circumstances as narrated above, confers no right upon the respondent for asking for stay of the execution of the decree. Both the trial court and the first revisional court, namely the Additional District Judge, observed that the respondent-tenant was making deliberate obstruction to execution of the decree for ejectment by filing the application for stay of execution of the decree. The learned Additional District Judge further observed that stay of a proceeding is discretion of the court and that when that discretion was exercised in this case by the trial court on sound judicial principle, revisional court got no jurisdiction to interfere. The learned Single Judge has observed that execution of the decree will seriously prejudice the judgment-debtor, plaintiff. There can hardly be any question raised as to prejudice to the judgment debtor when a lawful decree is put into execution. Moreover, disposal of the revisional application on merits giving the relief sought for resulted in the reversal of the order of the Additional District Judge without hearing the opposite party. This is illegal, unfair, unjust and improper. We strongly disapprove of disposal of revisional applications in this manner.</u>

5. In the result, the appeal is allowed, the impugned order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the Additional District Judge is restored. Since none has appeared for the respondent no order as to costs is made.

End.

full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J: This appeal is directed against the order of summary rejection of the High Court Division, Sylhet Bench, passed in Civil Order No. 65 of 1985, affirming the order of the Munsif, Sreemongal Upazila Court, dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1983 under Order XXI Rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure for willfully violating the order of injunction in Title Suit No. 374 of 1976 of the said Court.

2. The petitioner-appellant filed the above Title Suit against the opposite party and others for permanent injunction. In the said suit, the appellant alleged that he is the co-sharer and recorded owner of the suit Plot No. 287 and has been in exclusive possession of the same an amicable partition. The respondent having threatened to interfere with his peaceful possession and enjoyment in the suit land, he filed the suit and prayed for temporary injunction against the opposite party.

3. The respondent as defendant contested the said suit and the application for temporary injunction contending, inter alia, that the proforma defendants in the suit, who were plaintiff's co-sharers, owned Plot No. 387 by amicable partition with the plaintiff; that the said proforma defendants entered into a contract with the respondent for sale of 62 decimals of land in Plot No. 287 and on receipt of consideration money delivered possession to him. Subsequently, the proforma defendants left this country without completing the sale deed and consequently the said property was declared as enemy property and the respondent took lease of the same from the Government.

4. The prayer for temporary injunction of the appellant in the suit was allowed on contest on 13.8.1977 and the respondent and others were restrained from taking possession of the suit land.

5. The said suit for permanent injunction was decreed experts on 26.7.79.

6. Thereafter the present appellant filed the Miscellaneous case against the respondent for willfully disobeying the said decree despite the objection of the appellant and entered into the suit plot on 9.3.82 and cultivated the same.

7. The respondent contested the Miscellaneous case by filling a written objection, contending, inter alia, that the order of temporary injunction in the said suit a talk of compromise took place between the parties in which it was decided that the respondent would not contest the suit and allow the appellant to secure the decree, and then the appellant would transfer. 62 decimals of land from the western portion of the suit land and that a swaranlipi was executed between the parties. It is further asserted by the respondent that the appellant did not register the document thought the respondent was in possession of the suit land from before and as such there was no willful violation of the decree of permanent injunction.

8. The learned Munsif found that the appellant obtained an ex-parte decree for permanent injunction in Title Suit No.374 of 1975 but the said decree was not executed and dismissed the Miscellaneous case.

9. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in revision affirmed the order of the learned Munsif and believed that the appellant failed to make out a case of willfully disobeying the order of injunction in the Miscellaneous case.

10. Leave was granted to consider whether there was willful disobedience of the Court's order and the decree brings the opposite parties within the mischief of law as contemplated under Order XXI, Rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>11. A reference to Order XXI, Rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that when against any party a decree for injunction is passed and he has the opportunity of obeying the decree and he willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced by detaining him in civil prison, or by the attachment of his property or by both. Thus it will be pertinent to consider whether the respondent had the opportunity to obey the decree and had willfully failed to obey the same. In this case, the appellant examined 3 witnesses and the respondent examined 4 witnesses. The learned trial Court considered the evidence of both the parties in extinction in the judgment wherein it was observed that after the passing of the order of temporary injunction in favour of the appellant there was a talk of compromise between the parties. The trial Court did not find any cogent reason to disbelieve this evidence and accepted the contention of the parties that there was a talk of compromise and solenama (Swaranlipi) was executed between the parties though not filed in the suit The trial Court also considered another material aspect that the suit land was recorded in the name of plaintiff's co-sharer and after the departure of the brother of the appellant, the respondent was in possession of 672 decimals of land in suit plot. The trial Court found that the respondent was already in possession before the declaration of the property as enemy property and as such the respondent did not willfully disobey the said order. Thus, the learned Munsif on consideration of evidence on record held that the respondent did not get any opportunity to disobey the decree for permanent injunction and in fact there was no willful disobedience of the order of the Court. This factual determination of the issue was affirmed by the learned Single Judge. Thus there was no apparent illegality in the impugned judgment.</u>

12. Consequently, this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossain, J:—This application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order dated 28-12-82 passed by the Additional District judge, 2nd Court, Sadar, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 185 of 1981 affirming those dated 20-4-1981 passed by the Munsif, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 203 of 1979

2. Dr. A. Z. A. Ahad predecessor of the opposite parties instituted Other Suit No. 197 of 1974 in the First Court of Munsif, Sadar, Chittagong against the petitioner and another as defendants for eviction and recovery of arrear rent. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant petitioner was a monthly varatia under the plaintiff in the premises in suit and other defendant was inducted by the petitioner. The petitioner-defendant filed written statement in the suit denying the relationship of landlord and tenant. The defendant also alleged that he was in possession in part-performance of a contract for sale with the plaintiff. The suit was ultimately decreed exparte on 18-5-76. The defendant-petitioner therefore filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 CP.C for setting aside the exparte decree on the ground of illness. This application was allowed by the learned Munsif. The plaintiff, however, came to this Court in Revision, and in C.R. No. 158 of 1976, by judgment dated 29-6-77, the exparte decree dated 18-5-76 was 224 maintained. Thereafter the petitioner-defendant instituted Other Suit No. 226 of 1977 in the same Court for declaration that the exparte decree dated 18-5-76 in Other Suit No. 197 of 1974 was fraudulent, illegal and null and void. The Other Suit No. 226 of 1977 was dismissed on the ground of maintainability by judgment and order dated 10-11-1981. The petitioner defendant preferred Other Appeal No. 381 of 1981 which was allowed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Chittagong on 25-2-1982 and the suit was remanded to the trial court for hearing on merits. Against the judgment and order dated 25-2-82 Civil Revision No. 703 of 1982 was preferred and the Civil Revision is pending in this Court. In the meantime, pursuant to the exparte decree dated 18-5-76 obtained in Other Suit No. 197 of 1974 the plaintiff decree-holder started Other Execution No. 16 of 1976 in the same Court. In the execution case, the petitioner-Judgment-debtor filed an application for stay of execution, but the learned Munsif by judgment and order dated 2-9-77 rejected the petitioner's prayer for stay. The petitioner moved this Court in Civil Revision No. 1141 of 1977 but at the time of hearing did not press the rule on merits and by judgment dated 10-2-1978, this court ordered that Other Suit No. 226 of 1977 be disposed of expeditiously, preferably within 3 months of the receipt of the order and further that Execution Case No. 16 of 1976 be stayed for a period of 3 months. Civil Revision No. 1068 of 1978 arose at the instance of the petitioner over rejection of an application for examination of a disputed receipt by Handwriting Expert in Other Suit No. 226 of 1977 and the rule issued in the Civil Revision was discharged on 17-1-1979 with the direction that Other Suit No. 226 of 1977 be disposed of expeditiously preferably within three months from receipt of the order of the court. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted another suit being Other Suit No. 76 of 1976 against Dr. A.Z.A. Ahad, predecessor of opposite-parties in the Court of Subordinate-Judge for declaration of title in the suit premises and the land thereof and obtained an order of stay of further proceedings of other Execution Case No. 16 of 1976 on 6-7-1977. Dr. A.Z.A Ahad moved this court in Civil Revision No. 922 of 1977, obtained a rule which was ultimately made absolute on 14-2-1979. This Court directed the First Court of Munsif, Chittagong to proceed with Other Execution case No. 16 of 1976. Thereafter, the petitioner-defendant Judgment-debtor filed an application under section 47 C.P.C. in Other Execution Case No. 16 of 1976, and that application which was registered as Misc. Case No. 203 of 1979 was dismissed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court by order dated 20-4-1981. The petitioner-Judgment-debtor preferred Misc. Appeal No. 185 of 1981 and the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong who heard the matter dismissed the appeal on 28-12-1983 affirming the order of the learned Munsif dated 20-4-1981. Being aggrieved, the petitioner-Judgment-debtor has come up with this application.

<u>3. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner has taken me through the judgment of the courts below and other relevant materials. The learned Advocate submits that the learned Courts below have misapprehended the law in taking the view that an executing court was not competent to stay execution on the ground that the decree sought to be executed was obtained fraudulently as because it would amount to going behind the decree. The learned Advocate submits that the petitioner Judgment-debtor had filed a separate suit in the same court for setting aside the decree on the ground of fraud, and the court stayed execution of the decree. The learned Advocate places reliance on the decision of the Munnujan Begum V. A. Samad Molla & others reported in 29 DLR (SC) 282. In the reported decision the Appellate Division has held that the provision of Order 21, rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives powers to the court, where a suit is pending in any court against the holder of a decree of such court on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, to stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided. In that very decision, the Appellate Division has observed that the authority which has been given to a court under Order 21, rule 29 of the Code to stay an execution proceeding is discretionary, but the court shall have to apply its judicial mind in making the order of stay for the purpose of protecting the interests of the decree-holder. The Appellate Division also observed that it is settled principle that the discretion of a court, the exercise of which is likely to affect a valuable right of a person acquired under the law of the country, must be exercised judicially and for the said purpose the court must be satisfied that there are very good reasons for withholding from the holder of the decree the fruits thereof. In view of the provision of Order 21, rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in view of the decision of the Appellate Division, I am inclined to hold that the Courts below were not correct in taking a view that the executing court was not competent to stay execution of the decree which was sought to be undone by the Judgment-debtor before the same court in a separate suit. However, the Judgment-debtor has sought to undo the decree on the ground that it was obtained on the basis of a false claim in his absence as he was prevented by illness from offsetting the suit and his plea that he was prevented by illness from contesting the suit has been negative in Civil Revision No. 1581 of 1976 arising out of an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. filed by the Judgment-debtor defendant to undo the impugned decree. It is evident that his suit had, prima facie, little chance of success. The petitioner-Judgment-debtor was not, therefore, entitled to get an order of stay of the execution. The impugned Judgment and order of the learned Additional Judge affirming those of the Munsif refusing to stay execution of the impugned decree do not call for any interference.</u>

<u>The application is, therefore, summarily rejected.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This application filed on 27-5-2013 praying for review of the judgment dated 14-3-2013 passed by a Division Bench of this Court discharging the Rule of Civil Revision No. 2367 of 2012. The Rule came up for hearing on 13-3-2013 when the matter was heard-in-part, thereafter judgment was delivered on 14-3-2013.

2. The aforesaid revision obtained against order No. 17 dated 28-5-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge 1st Court, Dhaka rejecting Title Execution Case No. 9 of 2010 arising out of Title Suit No. 30 of 1998. Title Suit No. 30 of 19987 was a suit for specific performance of contract in which defendant appeared and filed written statement on 22-3-1998 and 28-5-1998 plaintiff filed application under Order XII, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure for passing decree in favour of plaintiff on admission. This application came up for hearing on 31-5-1998. Learned Judge then passed order and decreed the suit on admission against defendant No.1 and exparte against the other defendants. Plaintiff put the decree into execution through Title Execution Case No. 9 of 2010 i.e. long after 12 years 14 days. Learned Judge after taking into consideration the decision of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Bank Ltd. vs Sangbad Daily Paper, 36 DLR (AD) 5, rejected Execution Case, as, as per Article 182 of the Limitation Act the decree having not been put into execution within 3 years of the decree, it is barred by limitation. Decree holder plaintiff thereafter moved before this Court in Civil Revision No. 2367 of 2012. This rule was taken up for hearing and it appears that learned Advocate for the petitioner was not present. A Division Bench of this Court discharged the rule on taking same view of the learned trial Judge and also relied on decision of 36 DLR (AD) 5 relied by the learned trial Judge and also considered the decision of the same subject in the case of Abdul Hakim vs Goleda Begum, 36 DLR (AD) 7. Review is taken against this decision of the High Court Division.

3. Mr Mahbubur Rahman, learned Advocate, appearing for the applicant/petitioner, submits that, judgment needs to be reviewed as it is not hit by Article 182 of the Limitation Act which is not applicable in the present case and further submits that the decree having been directing obligation to be performed, the period of limitation as calculated by the learned Judge being devoid of any substance, the judgment passed by this Court ought to be reviewed. Learned Advocate relied on the case of Narayan Nath Roy Chowdhury vs Heramba Chandra Roy Chowdhury, 49 CWN 254 wherein it is held as:

"That the application was within time having been made within twelve years from the date of default.

4. In the execution proceedings of a decree, the parties entered into a compromise whereby the decretal dues were adjusted at a certain figure and it was stipulated that if the judgment-debtors paid a lesser amount in a certain number of installments, the decree would be deemed to be satisfied but in default the decree-holder would be at liberty to execute the original decree. The judgment-debtor after paying a few installments defaulted. The decree-debtor, thereafter, made an application for execution of the original decree. This application was made beyond twelve years from the date of the original decree but within twelve years from the date of default."

5. Mr SM Abdur Rouf, learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party, on the other hand, submits that, neither trial court nor the High Court Division committed any illegality in rejecting the Execution Case as it was filed beyond the period of limitation as prescribed under Article 182 of the Limitation act and relied on decisions which we have already mentioned herein above.

6. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate of both the parties.

7. Suit was filed on 28-1-1998 for specific performance of a contract in which defendant-Opposite party filed written statement on 22-3-1998. Thereafter plaintiff filed application for passing a decree on admission after serving notice to defendant No. 1. This application was allowed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka as follows:-

অতএব, আদেশ হয় যে, অত্র মামলাটি আইনত রক্ষনীয় নয় বিধায় দোতরফা সুত্রে খারিজ করা হইল।

8. Mr Mahbubur Rahman, learned Advocate submits that this decree was not executed as it require mutating the name of defendant No. 1, and permission from RAJUK and thereafter remaining money would be paid and thereafter deed would be executed and registered.

9. If we accept the submissions of Mr Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Advocate, decree was not executed after completion of the aforesaid formalities and after payment of balance consideration money within 60 days. As per section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure decree ought to be put into execution at first, within 3 years i.e. earlier period as per section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

10. An application for execution has therefore to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act, the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 of the Code which prescribed the maximum period of limitation. If the execution petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is fatal.

11. Appellate Division in the decision reported in 16 BLD (AD) 73, the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Bank Ltd. vs Sangbad Daily Paper, 36 DLR (AD) 5 and the case of Lalji Raja and Sons vs Firm Hansroj Nathuram, AIR 1971 (SC) 974 and took the view that-

"Both prescribe the period of limitation for the execution of the decree. The Civil Procedure Code fixes the longest period, whereas the Limitation Act the earliest period to take the first step in execution and the subsequent steps known as steps-in-aid."

12. It was further observed as:

"An application for execution has, therefore to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 of the Code which prescribed the maximum period of limitation. If the execution petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is, to fail."

<u>13. Provisions of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, shortly CPC is controlled by the provision of Limitation Act. This section requires that the first application for execution must be presented within the prescribed period mention in Article 182 of the Limitation Act, shortly the Act. If any application filed after period of limitation, as in the instant case, if no explanation of delay given, the application shall be dismissed. This section can only be applied if there be a prior application filed as per Article 182 of the Act. In the case of ADC (Rev.) Pabna vs Md Abdul Halim Mia, 48 DLR (AD) 141, it is held that if any application for execution of a decree hit either by Article 182 of the Act or section 48 of the CPC, it is fatal: A decree holder is entitled to present in succession any number of applications for execution of the same decree and the court has no power to refuse execution, unless:</u>

<u>a) the application is barred by virtue of general principle of law analogous to those of res judicata; or</u>

<u>b) the application is barred under Act, section 182 of Limitation Ad; or</u>

<u>c) the execution of the decree is barred under section 48 CPC though the application for execution may not be barred under (a) or (b) above.</u>

<u>14. The general effect of Article 182 of the Act is to require the first application for execution of a decree of a court, not High Court, to be made within 3 years of the decree, decree holder if failed to apply the first application for execution of a decree within 3 years, then decree die and cannot be executed.</u>

15. Now to the other part of the proceedings in the revisional application. It appears that written statement was filed denying the plaint case, then how the decree on admission was obtained. No statement has been made to the effect that whether the decree holder took any step as per decree i.e. for completion of the formalities. It appears petitioner after obtaining the decree, after long 12 years 14 days put the decree into execution meanwhile the period for limitation as per Article 182 of the Limitation Act as well as section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure has gone away.

16. Order XLVII speaks for review of a judgment. It has been held by different court of the sub-continent that review is not a mere matter of idle formalities or procedure. Review can be gone into if decision is erroneous in law. It is further been held that review has very limited jurisdiction non-consideration of evidence or formalities non-consideration of submissions of the learned Advocate are no ground for review of a judgment.

17. On a reading of the review petition itself we find that the grounds taken are relating to the order passed by the learned Joint District Judge. Not a single ground has been taken in respect of any part of our judgment as why our judgment requires to be reviewed. We find no substance in the review application.

In the result, the application is rejected.

Communicate this order at once.

End.
